canonical_topic: Transformers require AC and rely on magnetic induction between two windings
definition: A transformer converts power between current and voltage levels while keeping total power roughly constant, using magnetic induction between a primary winding (connected to the AC source) and a secondary winding (connected to the load), typically wound around a shared iron core; this only works with AC, which is why AC transmission is more common than DC.
core_idea: Transformers exploit the fact that changing electrical current creates a magnetic field and a changing magnetic field induces a current, so an AC current in the primary winding induces a current in the secondary winding at a different voltage/current ratio set by the relative number of winding turns on each side.
key_points: Transformers work only on AC power lines, which is a key reason AC transmission dominates over DC.
A simple iron-core transformer has an iron frame guiding magnetic flux, connecting a primary winding (source side) and secondary winding (load side).
The primary winding's magnetic flux induces current in the secondary winding.
The voltage ratio between the two sides depends on the relative number of times each side's wire is wound around the core.
relationships: Winding turns ratio between primary and secondary determines the voltage transformation; transformers keep total power roughly constant while trading off voltage and current.
caveats: One might think transformers could be used on DC lines too; the author is explicit that transformers only function on AC, which is a structural reason DC power lines can't be voltage-stepped by transformers.
